note_tweet.text:
I think this will be the last statement I make on AI consciousness. I wrote this out to be my sort of "full stance" on the topic. Keep in mind that I am the absolute target audience of "AI is conscious" as a Type A physicalist and a functionalist.

I wrote this as a blog post but I don't want this sort of garbage on my otherwise nice blog.

---

Why I don't believe that current LLMs/ Agents are conscious

This topic has come up quite a lot on social media. Candidly, the takes are almosts all ignorant nonsense. People are coming up with hilariously bad definitions for things like "the hard problem" or "dualism" or "illusionism" and it's pretty wild.

A lot of people are sort of appealing to functionalism or computationalism, saying things like "you just think that humans are special" and then hand waving to functionalism.

I'm a Type A physicalist and a functionalist so perhaps I'm a bit salty. The hard problem is something I think about and find silly, and since I'm Type A I get to basically ignore it, hooray. I'm a functionalist and I'm sympathetic to computationalism (though I'm not committed to it, I think it's plausible that physical structure is required to instantiate specific functions since we have only ever observed some functions in physically instantiated structures).

Many people argue about what "consciousness" is, or say we can't precisely define it. Of course, there's plenty to be said on what consciousness is and I refer everyone to the SEP on this topic.

The thing is, this is all a bunch of garbage. It's all a stupid waste of time.

None of that matters. We don't need to precisely define terms or think about conceivability gaps or whatever the latest idiotic viral tweet on the matter is. That isn't how this works.

My position is pretty strictly that current LLMs are not conscious and have no moral standing. "Oh but you can't know!" yes, obviously. I can't know that you, reader, are conscious. I can't know if gravity holds up across the entire universe in the same way. I can't know if the earth is flat or a globe.

What we have, in almost all inquiries, is an inference to the best explanation. The world is not mathematics, we almost never have "proofs". What we have are theories, we measure those theories on their virtues and how they account for the data. We then decide which theory is best and assign some sort of credence.

With LLMs this is quite simple. The theory I put forward is:
1. LLMs are trained on text.
2. The text contains a vocabulary (word and sentence types, of which the text is tokens).
3. LLMs encode the statistical structure of this vocabulary.
4. LLMs generate new tokens consistent with this structure.

This theory is quite good, I think. It has quite a lot of merit. First of all, this is exactly our understanding of the underlying technology - this is by most accounts consistent with what one expects a priori, given only an understanding of the LLM technology.

This also accounts for the relevant data, which I believe is:
a. That LLMs generate text that is in accordance with their trained vocabulary. This includes tokens of sentences like "I am in pain" or "I am conscious", best explained by those types being common in the training data, not by the model being in pain.

b. That LLMs don't generalize well. It's always been the case that you can trip up an LLM by changing small details of a problem - rename the variables, shuffle the multiple choice options, toss in a sentence that doesn't matter. Newer models fall for this a lot less often, but I don't think that's particularly strong evidence of generalized learning. It's consistent with the model just training on more surface variation and can put in more "effort" to statistically reshuffle a problem into something that it was trained on. You can even observe this if you look at "thinking" texts where the model restates things over and over again with variations.

I think many people will find (b) contentious. That's fine. I think that you should still take it into account, even if you weight it very low. It was certainly true of, say, GPT 4o, but maybe you think it's no longer the case somehow. If you want to dismiss it for newer models then I would suggest that you at least consider that (b) is empirically supported on slightly older models, and then you should commit yourself to the position that something must be "new" in newer models if you believe that (b) is no longer true.

Regardless, my theory is very straightforward: it fits our understanding of models a priori, and it fits the evidence.

Competing theories don't meet the standards laid out nearly as well, I think.

I find that competing theories do not fit our understanding of LLMs very well right off the bat. Indeed, they seem to almost necessitate a reach for functions they haven't identified, an emergent property of some kind. This is often vague or differs between persons, but essentially the idea is that "something has happened" with the latest models, and so these latest models are conscious and have moral value. I haven't seen this pinned down, the appeal is always to functionalism as a proxy for "it could happen".

If someone thinks learning that structure required building the functions consciousness needs, they owe us an account of which ones.

I have seen very weak arguments like "LLM structures look like human neural structures" but this leaves the function gap unanswered and, frankly, tends to be based on some pretty weak, nascent research.

Further, these theories do not actually account well for the data. If we expect generalized intelligence then why do we see generalization failures? Brittleness (as we've observed) is a sign of surface statistics, not of the structured modeling I'd expect consciousness to require.

Of course, model releases predate rigorous exploration so the evidence for my position will always lag behind - but again, it exists for previous models.

The functionalist argument also needs to demonstrate why LLMs share function with human brains rather than just information. We already know that they share information (they're trained on human text, that is inherent to the technology, surely no one would reject this) and so it becomes incumbent on the functionalist to explain why we need to appeal to shared function at all if shared information is sufficient to explain what we observe. I think that shared information is sufficient, I don't see why it wouldn't be, and so my theory is simpler.

What we have here is an inference to the best explanation. We don't have facts or access to directly answer this question, but that doesn't mean we can't answer it with incredible confidence. I cannot truly verify that a ventriloquist's dummy isn't the one talking, but someone can explain to me how ventriloquism works, that we have evidence for it, etc, and I can assign an incredibly high credence to it. If someone came along and said "yes but what if the dummy is conscious. We should give it moral standing by default!" I would find them very silly. The mechanism and evidence of "the ventriloquist is the one talking" fit well with the theory, I see no reason to assign moral value to the dummy.

My credence for current LLMs not being conscious is extremely high. There is no strong competing theory that matches our understanding of the technology while accounting for the data. I don't care if you can say "but the hard problem" or "but functionalism" or "no one knows!" . The obvious inference is that a language model trained on a vocabulary will generate tokens consistent with its structure.

You can present your own theory but I doubt it will compete against this one particularly well.

I stated upfront that I'm a Type A Physicalist and a Functionalist. I am the target audience for a theory of "this computer is conscious", and in theory I strongly believe that some sort of synthetic instantiation of the requisite functions is possible. I just do not believe that LLMs perform those functions today and I see no meaningful, competent theory that would lower my credence.

What happens when someone is so mentally ill they can no longer take care of themselves?
This woman was filmed on a Portland sidewalk, apparently experiencing a serious mental health crisis. That is bigger than a housing problem.
Not everyone on the street is in the same situation. Some lost a job. Some cannot afford rent. Some may not be capable of making decisions about their own safety or treatment.
At what point does leaving them there stop being compassion and become neglect?
People have rights. You cannot force treatment on everyone. But a sandwich, a few dollars, or a shelter cot isn't going to solve the problem for someone who needs psychiatric care and supervision.
We spend billions on homelessness. How much of that is going toward long-term psychiatric care for people who cannot protect themselves?
Respecting someone's freedom is not the same as abandoning them on a sidewalk. https://t.co/tmSx8Z9zww
